entries.title: West Virginia judge rules in favor of “Big Three” drug distributors in Cabell opioid lawsuit
entries.summary:
U.S. District Judge David A. Faber rules Cabell County and Huntington did not prove distributors’ pain pills created public nuisance

West Virginia judge rules in favor of “Big Three” drug distributors in Cabell opioid lawsuit appeared first on Mountain State Spotlight, West Virginia's civic newsroom.
entries.content:
A federal judge has ruled Cabell County and Huntington did not prove that the nation’s three largest drug distributors caused a public nuisance by shipping huge amounts of painkillers to the West Virginia community. 

Lawyers and officials for those communities, one of the areas hardest hit by the drug crisis, sued the “Big Three” drug distributors, AmeriSourceBergen Drug Corp., Cardinal Health, Inc. and McKesson Corp. in 2017, alleging they’d fueled the epidemic and should have been better scrutinizing higher-volume pharmacy orders. 

The county and city had asked Senior U.S. District Judge David A. Faber to determine whether companies were culpable under public nuisance law, meaning the companies’ wrongful conduct caused damage to the surrounding area.

“Their theory of the case was essentially that the volume of opioids distributed was in and of itself unreasonable,” Faber wrote. “But how can it be unreasonable for a wholesale distributor of opioids to fulfill bulk orders for opioids that are used to fill prescriptions written by doctors in good faith?”

Faber said the municipalities had provided no evidence showing they were sending painkillers to pill mills, that they knew their pills were being diverted or that they knew how many pills “should” have been sent to the area.

“And while there is a natural tendency to assign blame in cases like these, they must be decided not based on sympathy, but on the facts and the law.”

The two communities were trying to secure the funds for a proposed $2.5 billion, 15-year plan to remedy at least some portion of the epidemic’s resulting damage, trauma and devastation. 

Paul Farrell, a lawyer for the city and county, said he will appeal. 

Faber said that a more appropriate remedy would be about $330 million of the proposed $2.5 billion, and it would need to be strictly focused toward help for people with addiction, not other areas of the plan like drug use prevention.

In fact, he wrote that only one part of the current proposal, drug take-back and safe storage programs, was actually targeted toward the alleged wrongful conduct, oversupply. 

This is the second time lawyers for Cabell County and Huntington have argued their case before Faber. Plaintiffs had appealed Faber’s original ruling to the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which sent a certified question to the West Virginia Supreme Court, asking whether public nuisance law applied. 

When the state Supreme Court refused to answer, the question went back to the 4th Circuit, which found it did, and could be applied broadly to opioid cases. The case was then sent back to Faber, who once again, ruled in favor of the distributors.  

Correction Nov. 19, 2026: An earlier version of this story said the judge’s ruling had been made on Thursday Nov. 19, instead of Wednesday, Nov. 18, and incorrectly listed the amount of money he said would be appropriate to repair the harm done to the community.
